name: Florentine Codex
info: The Florentine Codex is a 16th-century study of Aztec culture by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua collabourators, in twelve books of Nahuatl and Spanish text with more than 2,000 illustrations by native artists.

facts.made: Bernardino de Sahagún, a Spanish Franciscan friar, in partnership with Nahua elders and authors who were formerly his students at the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco; the illustrations were drawn by native artists
facts.form: A manuscript of 2,500 pages in twelve books, in three bound volumes, with a Nahuatl text, a Spanish text and pictures; the pages are generally in two columns, Nahuatl on the right and Spanish on the left
facts.where: Biblioteca Medicea-Laurenziana in Florence, Italy, as Palat. 218-220; earlier drafts survive in Madrid; scans are online at the World Digital Library and in the Getty Research Institute's Digital Florentine Codex
facts.known: A record of Aztec religion, society, economics and natural history; Book 12, the conquest told from the side of the conquered of Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco; Nahuatl interviews with elders; Nahua medicine and plant lore; illustrations by tlacuilo artists; Sahagún's methods as an early form of ethnography

t: Sahagún, a missionary who wanted to help friars understand and convert the Aztecs, worked with Nahua elders and former students for decades to record their religion, society, economy and natural world in their own language.
The work has three texts in one, Nahuatl, Spanish and pictures, and its twelve books run from the gods to the conquest of the Aztec Empire told from the point of view of the conquered.

Held in Florence and unknown to most scholars until the late eighteenth century, it was translated into English over thirty years and has been put online in full, and UNESCO inscribed it in its Memory of the World register in 2015.
dyk: Sahagún credited by name the Aztec doctors who dictated the sections on anatomy, disease and medicinal plants; he named more than a dozen of them. The Codex was drawn up by about twenty-two artists, a figure deduced from the different ways they drew eyes, profiles and the proportions of the body.
ev: Sahagún begins the project that becomes the Historia General
The final version of the Florentine Codex is completed
The Council of the Indies suggests teaching the Indigenous peoples in Spanish, and Spanish authorities require Sahagún to hand over his documents
Angelo Maria Bandini publishes a Latin description of the manuscript held in the Laurentian Library
Francisco del Paso y Troncoso receives permission from the Italian government to copy the text and illustrations
The Mexican government publishes a full-colour three-volume facsimile in a limited edition of 2,000
High-resolution scans of all volumes are added to the World Digital Library
UNESCO inscribes Sahagún's work in its Memory of the World register

sections.origins:
The Florentine Codex is a 16th-century ethnographic research study in Mesoamerica by the Spanish Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún. He originally titled it La Historia General de las Cosas de Nueva España, in English The General History of the Things of New Spain. He worked on it from 1545 until his death in 1590, in partnership with Nahua elders and authors who were formerly his students at the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco.

Sahagún was a missionary, and his writings were devoted to evangelising the Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica. He described the work as an explanation of the "divine, or rather idolatrous, human, and natural things of New Spain" and compared its body of knowledge to what a physician needs to cure a "patient" suffering from idolatry. He had three goals: to describe and explain Indigenous religion, beliefs, practices and deities, so that friars and others could understand the religion they meant to replace; to create a vocabulary of Nahuatl, with explanations of cultural origins and pictures; and to record the cultural inheritance of the Indigenous peoples of New Spain. These goals are at times in competition within the work.

Spanish authorities were also seeking information. In 1569 the Council of the Indies ordered the Viceroyalty of New Spain to report on 37 chapters of ethnographic and geographic information, and in 1570 the requirement grew to 200 chapters. Philip II created the post of Cosmógrafo y Cronista Mayor de Indias and appointed Juan López de Velasco to it.
sections.content:
The Codex is essentially three texts in one: a Nahuatl text, a Spanish text and pictures. The pages are generally in two columns, with the Nahuatl, written first, on the right and a Spanish gloss or translation on the left. It documents the culture, religious cosmology and ritual practices, society, economics and natural history of the Aztec people. Its twelve books are The Gods; The Ceremonies; The Origin of the Gods; The Soothsayers; The Omens; Rhetoric and Moral Philosophy; The Sun, Moon and Stars, and the Binding of the Years; Kings and Lords; The Merchants; The People; Earthly Things; and The Conquest.

Book 8 deals with kings and lords and how they held elections and governed. Book 9 concerns the long-distance elite merchants, the pochteca, who expanded trade, reconnoitred new areas to conquer and served as agents-provocateurs. Book 10 describes the vices and virtues of all manner of persons, with human anatomy, disease and medicinal plant remedies, and also some other Indigenous groups of Mesoamerica. Book 11, Earthly Things, has the most text and about half of the drawings; the text calls it a "forest, garden, orchard of the Mexican language" and covers animals, birds, insects, fish, trees, minerals, mining, bridges, roads, terrain and food crops. Book 12 tells the conquest of the Aztec Empire from the point of view of the conquered of Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco and is the only strictly historical book of the Historia General.
sections.making:
Sahagún gathered knowledge in Nahuatl from people recognised as having expert knowledge of Aztec culture. According to the historian James Lockhart, he collected statements from Indigenous people of "relatively advanced age and high status, having what was said written down in Nahuatl by the aids he had trained". He compared the answers of different sources. Some passages seem to be transcriptions of spontaneous narration, others clearly answer a consistent set of questions put to different people, and some report Sahagún's own narration or commentary. Because many passages describe like items, such as gods, classes of people or animals, by consistent patterns, scholars have concluded that he used questionnaires, for example on a god's titles, powers, ceremonies and attire.

The manuscript was assembled, edited and appended over decades. In one of the prologues Sahagún takes full responsibility for dividing the Nahuatl text into books and chapters, late in its development, about 1566 to 1568. Scholars have proposed that Aristotle, Pliny the Elder, Isidore of Seville and Bartholomeus Anglicus inspired him, and one has argued, on circumstantial evidence, that Bartholomew's De proprietatibus rerum was a conceptual model.

The nearly 2,500 images were made as part of the work, about 2,000 of them "primary figures" that amplify the text and the rest ornamental. They were drawn in black outline, with colour added later. One scholar posits that they were made by members of the hereditary profession of tlacuilo, native scribe-painters. Scholars have concluded that twenty-two artists of varying skill worked on them. European elements appear beside pre-Conquest images in the native style, and some have Christian elements, which Peterson has called "Christian editorializing".
sections.reception:
The work reached the Spanish court in an unwelcome climate. In 1575 the Council of the Indies suggested educating the Indigenous peoples in Spanish instead of using their languages, and the Spanish authorities required Sahagún to hand over all his documents and research on Aztec culture. Philip II concluded that a general history of this kind was not beneficial for the Spanish colonies, and it never took place. Missionaries, Sahagún among them, continued their work, and he was able to make two more copies of his Historia general.

Copies were sent by ship to the royal court of Spain and to the Vatican in the late sixteenth century, and were then essentially lost for about two centuries. A scholarly community of historians, anthropologists, art historians and linguists has since investigated the work for more than 200 years.

Modern scholars judge its methods and its scope highly. Historians claim that Sahagún was the first anthropologist, and he has been given the title "Father of American Ethnography", though foremost in his own mind he was a Franciscan missionary. One scholar holds that the scope of the Historia's coverage of contact-period Central Mexican Indigenous culture is "unmatched by any other sixteenth-century works that attempted to describe the native way of life". Because it combines Nahua and European elements, voices and opinions, the document is sometimes contradictory, and modern readers may find the mixing of ways of presenting material confusing.
sections.survival:
The three bound volumes are in the Biblioteca Medicea-Laurenziana in Florence, as Palat. 218-220. The manuscript entered the Laurentian Library's collection at some point after its creation in the late sixteenth century. Scholars became aware of it only in the late eighteenth century, when the bibliographer Angelo Maria Bandini published a description of it in Latin in 1793. P. Fr. Marcellino da Civezza published a description in 1879, and the work became more generally known in the nineteenth century. The Spanish Royal Academy of History learned of it, and the find was announced to the wider scholarly community at the fifth meeting of the International Congress of Americanists. In 1888 Eduard Seler presented a description of the illustrations at the seventh meeting, and in 1893 Francisco del Paso y Troncoso received permission from the Italian government to copy the alphabetic text and illustrations.

The Codex has been compared with earlier drafts found in Madrid. The Tolosa Manuscript, the Códice Castellano de Madrid, was known in the 1860s and studied by José Fernando Ramírez, and it has been the source of all published Spanish editions of the Historia General. The title Florentine Codex was chosen by the English translators Arthur J. O. Anderson and Charles Dibble, following Mexican scholars of the nineteenth century. Blank spaces left for images, some never filled, suggest the manuscripts were still unfinished when they were sent to Spain.
sections.legacy:
Charles E. Dibble and Arthur J. O. Anderson were the first to translate the Codex from Nahuatl to English, in a project that took 30 years; it is regarded as an important contribution to the scholarship on Mesoamerican ethno-history. James Lockhart translated Book 12 separately in 2004, in We People Here: Nahuatl Accounts of the Conquest of Mexico. Books 10 and 11, on medicine and botany, were published by Sergii Kupriienko in 2013.

The Mexican government's facsimile of 1979, in a limited edition of 2,000, let scholars see the illustrations in detail for the first time; before that they were known mainly through black-and-white drawings separated from the text. In 2012 high-resolution scans of all volumes, in Nahuatl and Spanish with illustrations, were added to the World Digital Library. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed Sahagún's work in its Memory of the World register, and in 2023 the Getty Research Institute released the Digital Florentine Codex, which gives access to the complete manuscript and several translations.

The information on Nahua medicine is a major contribution to the history of medicine, and the sections on plants and animals are useful for the history of botany and zoology. Its pictures are regarded as a third column of language beside the Nahuatl and Spanish text.

summary: The Florentine Codex is the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún's General History of the Things of New Spain, written with Nahua elders and former students in Nahuatl and Spanish with some 2,000 illustrations. It records Aztec religion, society and nature and the conquest told by the conquered.
references: Bernardino de Sahagún, The Florentine Codex: General History of the Things of New Spain, translated by Arthur J. O. Anderson and Charles E. Dibble, 12 volumes (University of Utah Press, 2002)
notes: The article gives the work's length as 2,500 pages in the lead and 2,400 pages elsewhere; the facts line uses 2,500 as the lead has it, and the sections give no other figure.

The article gives about 2,000 illustrations in the lead and 'nearly 2,500' images (about 2,000 primary figures plus ornamentals) in the images section; the text uses 'more than 2,000' in info and the 2,500/2,000 split in the making section.

The article says Sahagún worked on the project from 1545 to his death in 1590, yet also says the final version was completed in 1569 and that the Nahuatl text was divided into books about 1566 to 1568; both are given as the article gives them. The article also says Sahagún made two more copies after Philip II's decision, without a date.
The article lists the books under three groupings (gods and religion; humanity; natural and general history) that do not map cleanly onto the twelve titles, so the groupings were left out.
The article's Book 8 to 10 descriptions are partly garbled (Book 10 'The People' is called 'general history'); the content section follows the titles and the article's own descriptions.

The 1575 Council of the Indies passage is muddled in the article (a 1568 order to Peru, Ovando, Sanchez); only the clearer points were used. The 1569 and 1570 chapter requirements are given as stated.

Left out: the claim that Sahagún was 'the first anthropologist' is attributed to historians; the article's 'one of the most remarkable social science research projects' wording was left out as praise.
References are the editions the article lists; it has no separate bibliography.
